blocks.name: Joint (<term d="A joint — the place where two bones meet.">articulation</term> / arthrosis)
blocks.def: A union or junction between two or more bones or rigid parts of the skeleton, allowing the rigid skeleton some flexibility. Each joint has a normal range of motion maintained by bony surfaces, cartilages, ligaments, tendons, and muscles working together.

blocks.name: Arthrology
blocks.def: The study of joints.

blocks.name: Arthroplasty
blocks.def: Surgical joint reconstruction or replacement.

blocks.name: Arthrocentesis
blocks.def: Aspiration of fluid from a joint.

blocks.x: Joints can be classified two ways: by function (how much movement they allow) or by structure (what separates/binds the articulating bones).

blocks.name: Synarthrosis
blocks.def: An immovable joint. Examples: suture, gomphosis, synchondroses.

blocks.name: Amphiarthrosis
blocks.def: A slightly movable joint. Examples: symphysis, syndesmosis.

blocks.name: Diarthrosis
blocks.def: A freely movable joint. All synovial joints fall into this category.

blocks.name: Fibrous joints
blocks.def: Bones connected by tough fibrous material; no joint cavity.

blocks.name: Cartilaginous joints
blocks.def: Bones united by <term d="A firm but flexible connective tissue that cushions joints and shapes structures like the ear.">cartilage</term>; no joint cavity.

blocks.name: Synovial joints
blocks.def: Bones separated by a fluid-filled joint cavity.

blocks.name: Synostosis
blocks.def: A "bony joint" — where two bones fuse and the boundary between them disappears entirely.

blocks.name: Suture
blocks.def: Joint held together by very short interconnecting fibers, with interlocking bone edges. Found only in the skull.

blocks.name: Gomphosis
blocks.def: A "peg-in-socket" fibrous joint — the periodontal <term d="A tough band of fibrous tissue that joins one bone to another.">ligament</term> holds a tooth in its socket.

blocks.name: Syndesmosis
blocks.def: Bones bound by a sheet (interosseous membrane) or bundle (interosseous ligament) of dense <term d="The tissue that supports, binds and separates other tissues, rich in matrix between its cells.">connective tissue</term> — e.g. between the tibia and fibula.

blocks.name: Synchondroses (primary cartilaginous joints)
blocks.def: Bones united by hyaline cartilage. Most are temporary structures that disappear during growth (e.g. the epiphyseal plate). Examples: 1st sternocostal joint, epiphyseal plates, costochondral joints.

blocks.name: Symphyses (secondary cartilaginous joints)
blocks.def: Bones united by fibrocartilage. Examples: the manubriosternal joint, the pubic symphysis, and intervertebral joints (via the fibrocartilaginous intervertebral disc).

blocks.cap: The general structure of a typical <term d="A freely movable joint with a fluid-filled cavity between the bone ends.">synovial joint</term>.

blocks.name: Articular cartilage
blocks.def: Covers the ends of the opposing bones; thickness decreases with age; acts as a shock absorber and reduces friction.

blocks.name: Joint (synovial) cavity
blocks.def: The space between articulating bones, filled with <term d="The slippery fluid inside a joint cavity that lubricates and nourishes the cartilage.">synovial fluid</term>.

blocks.name: Articular (joint) capsule
blocks.def: Encloses the joint cavity; has an outer fibrous capsule (dense irregular connective tissue, strengthens the joint) and an inner synovial membrane (loose connective tissue, lines the capsule, produces synovial fluid).

blocks.name: Synovial fluid
blocks.def: A colourless, viscous fluid that provides nutrients to structures in the joint cavity, contains phagocytes that remove microbes and debris, acts as a lubricant, maintains joint stability, cushions the joint under compression, and helps prevent the bone ends from separating — much like a film of water between two glass surfaces.

blocks.name: Accessory structures of synovial joints
blocks.def: Fat pads, menisci, ligaments, bursae, and tendons found at many synovial joints, alongside sensory nerves and blood vessels supplying the capsule and surrounding muscles.

blocks.name: Bursa
blocks.def: A synovial fluid-filled sac ("purse") occurring where ligaments, muscles, skin, tendons, or bones overlie and rub against each other. Reduces friction and cushions structures, facilitating movement of tendons/muscles over bone or ligament. Inflammation is called bursitis.

blocks.name: <term d="A strong cord of fibrous tissue that attaches muscle to bone.">Tendon</term> sheath
blocks.def: An elongated bursa that wraps around the tendons of certain muscles subjected to friction. Inflammation is called tenosynovitis.

blocks.cap: Synovial joint types by articulating surface shape (part 1: plane, hinge, pivot).

blocks.name: Plane joint
blocks.def: Formed when two flat surfaces meet, allowing gliding/sliding movement. Examples: intertarsal, intercarpal, 2nd–7th sternocostal, acromioclavicular, zygapophyseal joints.

blocks.name: Hinge (ginglymus) joint
blocks.def: A convex surface fits into a concave surface, allowing movement in a single plane only (uniaxial) — <term d="A movement that decreases the angle at a joint, bending it.">flexion</term> and <term d="A movement that increases the angle at a joint, straightening it.">extension</term>. Examples: elbow, knee, ankle, interphalangeal joints.

blocks.name: Pivot (trochoid) joint
blocks.def: A round surface fits into a ring formed by a ligament and a bony depression, allowing uniaxial rotation. Examples: <term d="Nearer to the trunk or to the point where a limb attaches.">proximal</term> radio-ulnar joint, atlanto-axial joint.

blocks.cap: Synovial joint types by articulating surface shape (part 2: saddle, condyloid, ball-and-socket).

blocks.name: Saddle joint
blocks.def: Bones with both concave and convex surfaces meet at right angles to each other, giving biaxial movement (flexion, extension, <term d="Movement of a body part away from the midline of the body.">abduction</term>, <term d="Movement of a body part back toward the midline of the body.">adduction</term>, <term d="A circular movement combining flexion, extension, abduction and adduction.">circumduction</term>). Example: 1st carpometacarpal joint (thumb opposition).

blocks.name: Condyloid (ellipsoid) joint
blocks.def: A convex oval surface fits into an elliptical concavity, giving biaxial movement. Examples: metacarpophalangeal (knuckle) joints, temporomandibular joint, radiocarpal (wrist) joint.

blocks.name: Ball-and-socket (spheroid) joint
blocks.def: A spherical head fits into a concave socket, giving multiaxial movement — flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, and circumduction. Examples: shoulder and hip joints.

blocks.name: Shape of articulating surfaces
blocks.def: Can prevent movement in specific directions, contributing to joint stability.

blocks.name: Ligament number & positioning
blocks.def: The more numerous and appropriately positioned the ligaments around a joint, the greater its stability.

blocks.name: Muscle tone
blocks.def: The baseline tension in relaxed muscle, important for maintaining posture and joint stability.

blocks.name: Sprain
blocks.def: Tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule.

blocks.name: Strain
blocks.def: Overstretching or tearing of a muscle or its tendon.

blocks.name: Dislocation (luxation)
blocks.def: Complete displacement of the articulating bone ends from their normal position.

blocks.name: Subluxation
blocks.def: A partial dislocation.

blocks.name: RICE protocol
blocks.def: Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation — the standard initial management for many joint/soft-tissue injuries.

blocks.name: Arthritis
blocks.def: A form of rheumatism in which joints are swollen, stiff, and painful. Causes include infectious agents, metabolic disorders, trauma, and immune disorders. The most common types are rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis; gouty arthritis is caused by uric acid crystal deposition in joints.

blocks.x: A ball-and-socket synovial joint between the head of the humerus and the glenoid fossa of the scapula — the most mobile joint in the body, but also the least stable, since the glenoid cavity is shallow relative to the large humeral head (roughly a 1:4 disproportion in articulating surfaces).

blocks.name: Glenohumeral ligaments
blocks.def: Superior, middle, and inferior bands that stabilize the anterior aspect of the shoulder joint, alongside the capsular, coracohumeral, and transverse humeral ligaments.

blocks.name: Rotator cuff
blocks.def: The sheath of tendons from the short shoulder muscles (subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, infraspinatus) that covers and blends with most of the joint, providing most of its stability. The supraspinatus is the strongest of these.

blocks.name: Glenoid labrum
blocks.def: A fibrocartilaginous ring that deepens the glenoid cavity, increasing the shoulder's stability.

blocks.name: Shoulder dislocation
blocks.def: The most common joint dislocation, most often occurring anteriorly (~95% of cases, vs. ~4% posterior and ~1% inferior). Can injure the axillary nerve (causing deltoid paralysis and loss of sensation over the "regimental badge" area) or, with downward displacement, stretch the radial nerve.

A synovial joint made of three distinct articulations working together within one joint capsule:

blocks.name: Humero-ulnar joint
blocks.def: Between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna; a hinge joint.

blocks.name: Humeroradial joint
blocks.def: Between the capitulum of the humerus and the head of the radius.

blocks.name: Superior radio-ulnar joint
blocks.def: Between the head of the radius and the radial notch of the ulna, held in place by the annular ligament; a pivot joint.

blocks.name: Medial collateral ligament (elbow)
blocks.def: Made of anterior oblique, transverse, and posterior oblique bands; the anterior oblique band is the main stabilizer, resisting excessive valgus (outward) force and internal rotation stress.

blocks.name: Lateral collateral ligament complex (elbow)
blocks.def: Consists of the radial collateral ligament, the annular (orbicular) ligament, the accessory lateral collateral ligament (stabilizes the annular ligament during varus stress), and the lateral ulnar collateral ligament (the main stabilizer) — together protecting against varus (inward) force.

blocks.name: Varus vs. valgus
blocks.def: Terms describing angulation of a bone/joint in the <term d="A vertical cut running side to side that divides the body into front and back parts.">coronal plane</term>, based on whether the <term d="Further away from the trunk or from the point where a limb attaches.">distal</term> part sits more medial (varus) or more lateral (valgus) than normal.

blocks.name: Elbow bursae
blocks.def: Intratendinous (within the triceps tendon), subtendinous (between the olecranon and triceps tendon), and subcutaneous/olecranon bursa (between the olecranon and overlying skin — implicated in olecranon bursitis, aka "student's elbow").

blocks.name: Carrying angle
blocks.def: The acute angle between the long axis of the arm and forearm in full extension/<term d="Rotating the forearm so the palm faces upward or forward.">supination</term>, letting the forearm clear the hips while walking — important for carrying objects.

blocks.name: Epicondylitis
blocks.def: Inflammation of the tendons around the elbow from overuse. Medial epicondylitis = "golfer's elbow"; lateral epicondylitis = "tennis elbow."

blocks.name: Supracondylar fracture
blocks.def: A fracture just above the elbow, typically from a fall onto an outstretched hand; can damage the median, ulnar, or radial nerve, and may lead to Volkmann's ischaemic contracture (uncontrolled hand flexion from fibrotic, shortened flexor muscles).

blocks.name: Radial head subluxation ("nursemaid's elbow")
blocks.def: The radial head is traumatically pulled out of the annular ligament, typically in young children from a sudden pull on the extended arm.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The Elbow JointCovers the three articulations of the elbow and its supporting ligaments.

blocks.name: Hip joint (structure)
blocks.def: A ball-and-socket synovial joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the os coxae, deepened by a fibrocartilaginous rim called the acetabular labrum.

blocks.name: Ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur)
blocks.def: An intracapsular ligament running from the acetabular fossa to the fovea of the femoral head, enclosing a branch of the obturator artery. Rupture can damage this artery and cause avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

blocks.name: Iliofemoral ligament
blocks.def: The strongest ligament in the body; arises from the anterior inferior iliac spine, bifurcates into a Y-shape, and inserts on the intertrochanteric line — prevents hyperextension of the hip while standing.

blocks.name: Pubofemoral ligament
blocks.def: Spans from the superior pubic rami to the intertrochanteric line, reinforcing the capsule anteroinferiorly; prevents excessive abduction and extension.

blocks.name: Ischiofemoral ligament
blocks.def: The weakest of the hip's three extracapsular ligaments; runs from the ischium to the greater trochanter, reinforcing the capsule posteriorly and preventing hyperextension.

blocks.name: Hip joint innervation
blocks.def: Supplied by the sciatic, femoral, and obturator nerves. Because the femoral nerve also supplies the front/medial thigh skin, and the obturator nerve supplies both hip and knee joints, hip disease can refer pain to the thigh or knee.

blocks.name: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH)
blocks.def: A shallow acetabulum from failure to develop properly in utero, causing limited hip abduction, limb length discrepancy, and asymmetrical gluteal/thigh skin folds; treated with a Pavlik harness.

blocks.name: Acquired hip dislocation
blocks.def: Usually from trauma or as a complication of hip replacement surgery. Posterior dislocation (~90%) is most common since the joint is least stable when flexed and adducted, and can injure the sciatic nerve; anterior dislocation is rare.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: The Hip JointThe hip's ball-and-socket structure, ligaments, and stability compared to the shoulder.

blocks.name: Knee joint (structure)
blocks.def: A modified hinge joint — the largest and most complex joint in the body. Consists of two articulations sharing one joint cavity: the tibiofemoral (condylar) joint and the patellofemoral (saddle) joint. The tibial condyles are clinically called the medial and lateral tibial plateaus.

blocks.name: Tibial (medial) collateral ligament (MCL)
blocks.def: Thicker and stronger than the LCL; attached to the medial meniscus (so MCL injury often involves meniscus injury too); resists valgus-producing forces.

blocks.name: Fibular (lateral) collateral ligament (LCL)
blocks.def: Thinner and rounder than the MCL; resists varus-producing forces.

blocks.name: Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL)
blocks.def: Blends with the medial meniscus; the weaker and more commonly injured of the two cruciate ligaments; limits knee hyperextension and prevents anterior dislocation of the tibia on the femur.

blocks.name: Posterior cruciate ligament (PCL)
blocks.def: Stronger, shorter, and broader than the ACL; limits knee hyperflexion and prevents posterior dislocation of the tibia on the femur.

blocks.name: Menisci (knee)
blocks.def: Fibrocartilage structures that deepen the tibial articular surface, increase stability, and act as shock absorbers by spreading load across a larger surface area. Each attaches to the tibia via anterior and posterior horns.

blocks.name: Medial meniscus
blocks.def: Nearly semicircular (C-shaped), broader posteriorly; attached to the MCL and joint capsule, making it relatively immobile and more prone to injury.

blocks.name: Lateral meniscus
blocks.def: About 4/5 of a circle; smaller and more mobile than the medial meniscus.

blocks.name: Prepatellar bursitis ("housemaid's knee")
blocks.def: Inflammation/swelling of the prepatellar bursa, from prolonged kneeling.

blocks.name: Infrapatellar bursitis ("clergyman's knee")
blocks.def: Inflammation of the (<term d="Closer to the surface of the body.">superficial</term>) infrapatellar bursa.

blocks.name: Anterior/posterior drawer sign
blocks.def: Clinical tests for cruciate ligament injury — the anterior drawer sign indicates an ACL tear (tibia pushed anteriorly); the posterior drawer sign indicates a PCL tear (tibia pushed posteriorly, a classic "dashboard injury").

blocks.name: "Unhappy triad" (terrible triad)
blocks.def: A combined knee injury involving the ACL, medial meniscus, and MCL — common in contact sports from a direct blow to the lateral knee during extension.

blocks.name: Q angle
blocks.def: The angle between the quadriceps' line of pull and the patellar tendon; an increased Q-angle is a risk factor for patellofemoral pain, patellar instability, and ACL injury; typically larger in females due to a wider pelvis.

blocks.x: ▶️Watch: Knee Joint Structure and ActionsStructure of the knee, its ligaments and menisci, and the movements it allows.

blocks.name: Ankle (talocrural) joint
blocks.def: A modified hinge joint formed by the malleoli, the inferior articular surface of the tibia, and the talus (the "ankle mortise"). Permits dorsiflexion and plantarflexion; stable in dorsiflexion, less stable in plantarflexion. Inversion/eversion occur at the tarsal joints, not the ankle joint itself.

blocks.name: Medial (deltoid) ligament
blocks.def: Fans out from the medial malleolus to the talus, calcaneus, navicular, and spring ligament; resists over-eversion of the foot. Stronger than the lateral ligament, so forced inversion sprains are more common than eversion sprains.

blocks.name: Lateral ligament (ankle)
blocks.def: Made of the anterior talofibular, posterior talofibular, and calcaneofibular ligaments, originating from the lateral malleolus; resists over-inversion. Weaker than the medial ligament — the anterior talofibular ligament is the weakest part and the most commonly injured in ankle sprains.
